project.name: Not Arbitrary 07 — Roman Numerals Are Not Letters

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Roman numerals are not letters. We read them as letters, and the Romans eventually did too. But every one was a shape before the alphabet got near it.
entries.direction: Warm, unhurried, slightly conspiratorial. The first sentence is the hook - state it flatly and let the pause do the work.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Start with a shepherd and a stick. Count the flock past you at dusk and cut one notch for each animal. That is the first numeral.
entries.direction: Plain and physical, as if describing someone at work. A small beat before the last sentence.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Reading a row of identical notches is slow work, so the fifth one gets a different cut, and the tenth gets cut clean across.
entries.direction: Practical, matter of fact. Land 'across' crisply.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Lift that crossed notch off the wood and put it on a page. Nothing has changed. That is still the cut for ten, straight out of the wood.
entries.direction: Quiet satisfaction. Do not push the reveal - let the middle sentence sit.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Cutting a sign in half is not a trick played once. It is the rule the whole system runs on, long after the stick itself is gone.
entries.direction: Building slightly. This is the promise the rest of the film pays off.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Rome learned to count from the Etruscans, who wrote a hundred as a star. Cut the star in half and their fifty is what is left.
entries.direction: Conversational. Pronounce Etruscans clearly, ih-TRUS-kans, and do not carry that colour into the next word.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Press that half flat, slide its stem out to the end, and an ordinary Latin letter is standing there holding a number far older than itself.
entries.direction: One continuous thought, no pause until the end. Slight lift on 'older'.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: The large numbers were built, not cut. A thousand was an arc, a stroke, and a second arc turned back the other way.
entries.direction: Deliberate, one item at a time, as if drawing each mark while speaking.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Push those three together and they close into a ring. Open it out again in a hurry, with a pen rather than a chisel, and there is the letter we still use.
entries.direction: Unhurried through the middle, then land the final clause with quiet certainty. Open on a clean firm P in 'Push' - do not soften it into a K.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Rome halved its big signs exactly as it halved the small ones, because half a sign for half a number costs nothing to remember.
entries.direction: Even and explanatory. The picture is doing the reveal here, so stay out of its way.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: So here is what actually happened. The shapes came first, off a stick and out of Etruria. The letters drifted in later, because they looked alike.
entries.direction: This is the turn. Slow down. Pronounce Etruria as ih-TROOR-ee-uh and keep the following words clean of it.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: You were probably taught that the hundred stands for centum and the thousand for mille. Both words do mean that. Neither one explains the shape.
entries.direction: Gentle, not smug. Latin centum as KEN-tum and mille as MIL-lay, each finished before the next English word begins.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: None of this was designed. It was cut, halved, closed and opened again by people who needed to count things long before they thought to spell them.
entries.direction: Warm summary. Let the list of verbs breathe.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: So when you next meet a date written this way, do not read it as Latin. Read it as a stick with cuts in it.
entries.direction: Land it softly and stop. Do not rush the final sentence.
